newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris flaunts profitability despite woes.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris flaunts profitability despite woes.

text.p: Philip Morris Cos Inc, flush with cash from its tobacco business, boosted its dividend by 20 percent on Wednesday, giving it one of the most lucrative dividend yields among big companies on Wall Street.
Analysts said the decision was not a panic move in response to the legal and regulatory woes besetting the tobacco industry, but rather was a reflection of the company's profitability and confidence.
Martin Feldman, of Smith Barney, called the move "excellent," and said Wall Street's concerns over litigation and government regulation do not appear to be shared by the company.
"It indicates a strength of operating performance as well as the company's belief in the inherent strength of the defenses on the litigation front," Feldman said.
Philip Morris's yield of 5.2 percent is now two and a half times that of the Standard & Poor's 500 index.
The new quarterly payout of $1.20 per share, up from $1.00, was right on target with Wall Street's expectations.
Philip Morris closed Wednesday at 91-1/4, off 5/8, on more than 2.7 million shares traded.
Roy Burry, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, said some on Wall Street had expectations of an increase to $1.25, or $5 annually, and that disappointment was the cause of Wednesday's price drop.
But a dividend hike that large - 25 percent - would have been overreaching, Burry said. "That would have made the board (of directors) look like they were pushed into it," he said.

Although the company's stock price has fallen since an August 9 court ruling against the industry, the higher dividend was not intended only to bolster the share price, said Ronald Morrow, analyst at Rodman & Renshaw.

"It's no more, no less than what you would anticipate them to do with the kind of profit they're making. I don't think there's any statement here about fears, or any statement about anything," Morrow said.

Analysts had also anticipated a stock split would be announced with the dividend. When the price of company shares plunged about 20 percent after the unfavorable court ruling, the split was put off, analysts said.
"I would expect that once the stock has been (trading) above $100 for eight weeks or so, the company will announce a split," Feldman said.
"They didn't feel it necessary to shore up the stock price by giving an unduly aggressive dividend-per-share increase," he said.
Also not announced was an anticipated 1997 share repuchase program. Feldman said the buyback program's announcement was probably delayed so the company could spread out its good news.
He expects Philip Morris to set a repurchase program for $3 billion worth of stock in 1997, or a $6-billion program for 1997 and 1998 combined.
